headlines.article_text: Chevron CEO warns against 'unwise' diesel export ban Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Chevron CEO Mike Wirth told CNBC that a U.S. diesel export ban would be “unwise,” saying it could worsen supply pressures and undermine confidence in the U.S. as a reliable energy supplier. Global supply fears have eased following higher Middle East crude exports and a G7 emergency stockpile release, but markets remain on edge as the U.S.-Iran war drags on. In this article CVX Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 6:20 06:20 Chevron CEO says low reserves leave energy system vulnerable to disruption Squawk Box Europe The chief executive of U.S. oil giant Chevron on Wednesday warned it would be "unwise" for the Trump administration to move forward with a diesel export ban , saying the policy runs the risk of making the supply situation worse. "The U.S. has been a reliable supplier to the world at a time when it needs it," Chevron CEO Mike Wirth told CNBC's " Squawk Box Europe " in an exclusive interview on Wednesday. "And I think it would be unwise for the U.S. to create questions in the minds of our allies and our partners as to whether or not we will be there with reliable supply when times are difficult — and so, there are other options," he added. His comments come as rising Middle East crude exports and an emergency G7 stockpile release appear to have helped to ease supply fears, although energy market participants remain on edge as Saudi Arabia and Iran-backed Houthi forces exchange attacks . The U.S.-Iran war has severely disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow waterway that typically handles around 20% of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas supplies, sending shock waves through the global economy. A sign displays the prices of unleaded gasoline and diesel fuel at a Chevron gas station in Bay Harbor Island, Florida, US, on Monday, June 22, 2026. Bloomberg | Bloomberg | Getty Images U.S. President Donald Trump , who has cooled on the prospect of authorizing a diesel export ban after G7 countries agreed to release diesel and crude oil from their emergency reserves, recently allowed the use of cheaper red-dyed diesel to be used more broadly in part of a push to bring down record-high fuel costs. Trump signed an executive order Monday evening stateside to temporarily allow truckers and farmers to use red-dyed diesel — which is exempt from highway fuel taxes — and deferred related taxes on the fuel through the end of this year. The tax-free diesel is typically used by farm equipment, construction machinery, trucks and other off-road vehicles. It is therefore exempt from a 24.4-cent-per-gallon tax applied to diesel fuel sold for highway transportation. Saudi Aramco CEO Amin Nasser said earlier this week that it could take up to two years to rebuild global oil inventories, warning that the squeeze on supplies could yet get worse as the U.S.-Iran war drags on. Energy system 'more vulnerable to disruption' Asked how fragile the global inventory position is ahead of winter, Chevron's CEO described it as a "very serious" situation. "We came into this year with high inventories. High inventories in commercial stocks held by companies, high inventories in strategic stocks held by governments around the world and actually significant inventories on the water, particularly barrels that were sanctioned by the U.S. or the EU," Wirth said. "Over the last several months, we've seen commercial inventories draw down, strategic stocks be released and those sanctioned barrels have been relieved and allowed to be delivered as well," he continued. "Those are all buffers in the system that have bought us time, but they've been drained. And so, we're at much lower levels of inventory right now and it makes the system more vulnerable to disruption." — CNBC's Anniek Bao contributed to this report. In this article TMCV-IN Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT The Jaguar Type 01 is revealed during the Jaguar Type 01 Launch Event at Storied NYC on October 06, 2026 in New York City. Noam Galai | Getty Images Entertainment | Getty Images Luxury carmaker Jaguar has launched its new all-electric vehicle, two years after the famed British company's controversial rebrand prompted a social media backlash. The automotive manufacturer, which is owned by India's Tata Motors , unveiled the Type 01 model on Tuesday at an event in New York City, describing it as the "most technically advanced" and "most powerful and aerodynamic" Jaguar ever. It marks a radical new direction for the company, which was criticized in November 2024 when it revealed a series of changes ahead of becoming a fully electric brand. Jaguar posted a 30-second clip on X at the time which featured several models in brightly colored clothing and marketing slogans such as "live vivid", "delete ordinary" and "copy nothing." Notably, the ad did not feature a car or the company's traditional cat logo. Among those to criticize the ad was Elon Musk , with the owner of the X social media platform asking : "Do you sell cars?" Jaguar sought to defend the ad campaign, telling Sky News at the time that the company wanted "to be bold and disruptive." Italy's Ferrari and Britain's Bentley have also launched their first EV models this year, seeking to test wealthy buyer's appetite for going electric as luxury carmakers seek to compete with cheaper Chinese car brands. Jaguar's Type 01 has a starting price of £130,000 (roughly $172,000) in the U.K. and around $130,500 in the U.S., according to multiple media reports , which is significantly higher than previous comparable models. The four-door "Grand Tourer" has an ultra-long bonnet, low roofline, frameless doors and a camera instead of a rear window. It has a range of up to 450 miles and can accelerate from 0-62 miles per hour in 3.2 seconds.
